per_claim_scores.claim_text: Mercer Marsh Benefits reported Indonesia's medical trend rate at ~13.6% (2023 MMB benchmark)
source_categories: primary_academic (Prastyo & Gani 2025 Narra J, PMC-indexed — cites 13.6% as MMB Indonesia benchmark)
per_claim_scores.rationale: The 13.6% figure is cited in the peer-reviewed Prastyo & Gani 2025 Narra J paper (PMC12425502) which independently cites the MMB Indonesia benchmark, AND the original MMB HBS 2024 source. Two independent primary-tier sources (peer-reviewed academic citing primary consultancy + the consultancy report itself). Aon 2026 adds a third top-tier consultancy for the 2026 projection (16.9%). Geography is Indonesia-specific. Data is recent (2023 benchmark). Strong claim.

per_claim_scores.claim_text: BPJS Kesehatan costs up to IDR 5.76 million/employee/year (at the IDR 12M cap); employer rate 4%, employee 1%
source_categories: secondary (Acclime Indonesia — accounting/advisory firm's published guide)
per_claim_scores.rationale: Acclime is an accounting advisory firm; their guides synthesize regulation but are secondary. The underlying regulation (PP No. 44/2015, PP No. 46/2015) is well-established and widely reported. The math (4% of IDR 12M cap = IDR 480,000/month × 12 = IDR 5.76M/year) is straightforward from the regulation itself. The draft correctly cites the regulatory basis in text (PP No. 44/2015 and PP No. 46/2015) but the footnote URL leads to Acclime's guide rather than the government regulation. Scores Medium — the underlying regulation is public law and the calculation is accurate, but the citation is advisory-firm secondary rather than the gazette or BPJS official site.

per_claim_scores.claim_text: Riskesdas 2023 shows diabetes prevalence of 11.3% in the general population and 4.6% in productive-age urban populations
source_categories: primary_academic (Dewi et al 2025, PMC12519354 — serial analysis of Riskesdas 2013, 2018, 2023)
primary_academic (Soewondo et al 2014, PMC4188107 — urban productive-age study)
per_claim_scores.rationale: The 11.3% figure comes from Dewi et al 2025 (PMC12519354) which is a peer-reviewed serial analysis of Indonesia's Riskesdas national health surveys — strong primary academic source. However: the draft conflates two different figures from two different papers/time periods. The 11.3% is from Riskesdas 2023 (cited via Dewi 2025); the 4.6% is from Soewondo 2014 (PMC4188107) — a 2014 study of urban productive-age adults, now 12 years old (outdated-source override: >3 years old). The claim pairs a current figure (11.3%) with an outdated figure (4.6%, 2014) without flagging the recency mismatch. Score: Medium — the 11.3% is well-sourced; the 4.6% is stale.

per_claim_scores.claim_text: OJK Circular Letter 7/SEOJK.05/2025 proposed mandatory 10% employee co-payment for inpatient and outpatient claims; implementation deferred pending formal POJK
source_categories: primary_consultancy (Aon Indonesia blog/insight — primary-consultancy authored analysis of OJK regulation)
per_claim_scores.rationale: Aon Indonesia is a top-tier consultancy; their published insights on OJK regulation are authoritative market commentary. However: this is an Aon blog/insight page rather than a firm-authored research report with named authors and methodology disclosure — it sits at the boundary of primary_consultancy and secondary. The underlying OJK Circular Letter itself (SEOJK.05/2025) is a primary_ministry document but no direct OJK gazette URL is cited. One consultancy source for a regulatory claim that should ideally cite the OJK circular directly. Borderline Medium.

per_claim_scores.rationale: The CIPD/AIA Asia Employee Benefits Report 2024 covers Hong Kong and Singapore primarily (n=409; 162 HK, 157 SG, 90 other countries of which Indonesia has negligible representation per Table 1 in the report). The report explicitly states: 'we have only conducted country-level analysis on Hong Kong and Singapore.' Using this report to support a claim about Indonesian employers is a geography mismatch. APAC-as-proxy override triggers: report is not Indonesia-specific. Even without the geography issue, the CIPD report does not specifically address the MCU-claims data disconnect. Auto-Low: Geography mismatch.

per_claim_scores.claim_text: Indonesian NCD economic burden estimated at $4.47 trillion in workplace productivity loss between 2012 and 2030; coronary heart disease alone accounts for 2.8% (absenteeism) and 6.8% (presenteeism) of annual GDP
source_categories: primary_academic (Tran/Uli et al 2020, BMC Cardiovascular Disorders, PMC7482464)
per_claim_scores.rationale: The Tran et al 2020 paper (PMC7482464) is peer-reviewed and Indonesia-specific (working Indonesian population life-table modelling). Strong primary academic source. However: the $4.47 trillion NCD productivity loss 2012–2030 figure is described in the draft as 'cited in secondary' — meaning it is not directly in PMC7482464. The 2.8% absenteeism and 6.8% presenteeism of GDP appear to be from this paper or its secondary citations. The '$4.47 trillion' NCD burden figure is a very large number (implausibly larger than Indonesia's entire GDP for the period unless cumulative discounted) — the draft's own footnote says 'cited in secondary' which means the primary paper may be reporting CHD-specific figures and the $4.47 trillion is an aggregation from elsewhere. Chain-of-citations flag: the $4.47 trillion figure needs direct source verification. Score: Medium for CHD-specific figures from the paper; the $4.47 trillion is unverified paraphrase chain.
overrides_triggered: chain-of-citations (the $4.47T NCD burden is noted as 'cited in secondary' — not directly from PMC7482464)

per_claim_scores.claim_text: 2016 BPJS-based cost-of-illness study found total direct medical costs of T2DM of US$576 million nationally; ~74% spent on patients with complications; inpatient cost was 56% of total
source_categories: primary_academic (peer-reviewed journal — Value in Health Regional Issues; uses BPJS claims data 2016)
per_claim_scores.rationale: Value in Health Regional Issues is a peer-reviewed journal (Elsevier). The study uses 2016 BPJS administrative data — now 9 years old. Outdated-source override: cost-of-illness figures from 2016 for healthcare costs (which inflate rapidly in Indonesia at 13–19%/year) are materially stale. Score drops from High to Medium due to recency issue. The paper is well-established academically, but the 2016 cost numbers significantly understate 2024/2025 reality.
overrides_triggered: outdated-source-override (2016 BPJS data; 9 years old; Indonesian medical costs have roughly doubled since then)

per_claim_scores.claim_text: MMB Indonesia HBS 2024 (n=470+ companies, 320,000+ members): average inpatient claim Rp 22 million / ~USD 1,419 per person in 2023; average outpatient claim Rp 3.6 million / ~USD 232 per person
per_claim_scores.rationale: ANTARA is Indonesia's state news agency — strong secondary, not trade press. The ANTARA article reports the MMB HBS 2024 figures (Rp 22M inpatient, Rp 3.6M outpatient) attributed to Marsh Indonesia at a public announcement. The underlying source (MMB HBS 2024) is primary_consultancy but gated. ANTARA reporting on a Marsh Indonesia press announcement is chain-of-citations: the primary is MMB HBS 2024, accessed via ANTARA secondary reporting of a press event. Score: Medium — credible secondary (ANTARA is authoritative news) plus gated primary consultancy source. Indonesia-specific and recent (2024 study).

per_claim_scores.claim_text: Cardiovascular and metabolic complications (stroke, AMI, renal disease) routinely cost Rp 100–400 million / USD 6,450–25,800 per episode in private hospitals
per_claim_scores.rationale: Single secondary news source for a quantified cost-per-episode claim. The Jakarta Post article (March 2024) is about rising medical costs generally and claims surge — it is not a hospital pricing study or insurer tariff study. Single-trade/news-source override for an operating cost figure. Private hospital episode cost for stroke/AMI/renal should be sourced from hospital tariff schedules, insurer claims data, or cost-of-illness studies. Single news source is insufficient.

per_claim_scores.claim_text: 94% of 470+ Indonesian companies surveyed (MMB HBS 2024) provide inpatient benefits; 79% provide outpatient benefits
per_claim_scores.rationale: Same sourcing as PP1.1-cost-2. ANTARA + gated MMB HBS 2024. Medium — same reasoning applies.

per_claim_scores.claim_text: Indonesia's 2025 medical trend rate is 19%, highest in Asia except Philippines (21%); Jakarta Post reported health insurance claims grew 25% YoY in 2023
per_claim_scores.rationale: The 19% figure appears in pain point 1.1 sourced only to the Jakarta Post article (source 4). The actual 19% MMB HTS 2025 source is cited in pain point 1.4 (source 2) but not cross-referenced here. The Jakarta Post article covers the 25% claims growth and 13.6% 2023 trend (from MMB HBS 2024). The 19% 2025 projection is from MMB HTS 2025 — if that source is not cited in this specific claim's footnotes, it is single-news-source for the 19% figure as presented here. However the broader draft does cite MMB HTS 2025 separately. Chain-of-citations: Jakarta Post cites AAJI for claims growth data. The claims growth figure (25% YoY) is AAJI data reported via Jakarta Post — the AAJI is a primary_association (Indonesia Life Insurance Association). Score: Medium for the 25% claims growth (strong secondary citing primary association); Low for 19% trend rate if only Jakarta Post cited here — treating as Low for this claim since sourcing in footnote 4 is Jakarta Post only.
overrides_triggered: single-trade-source (19% figure sourced only to Jakarta Post in this footnote set)

per_claim_scores.claim_text: Indonesia employer-sponsored health insurance medical cost inflation: 12.3% in 2022, 13.6% in 2023 (Jakarta Post / MMB 2024), accelerating to 19% projected 2025 (MMB HTS 2025)
source_categories: primary_consultancy (MMB HTS 2025 PDF hosted on fwd.co.id)
per_claim_scores.rationale: The MMB HTS 2025 PDF hosted on fwd.co.id is a Mercer Marsh Benefits authored report (firm-imprint document) — primary_consultancy, even though hosted on an insurer's site. The PDF URL pattern suggests a document library hosting of the MMB report. This is the strongest of the three sources and directly supports the 19% figure and trend series. Jakarta Post adds context for 13.6% (2023). HCA Magazine is redundant trade press citing the same MMB data. Score: Medium — one primary_consultancy source (MMB HTS 2025) plus secondary news. Would be High if the MMB report URL directly resolved to a Marsh-owned domain or if PMC academic corroboration existed for the trend series.

per_claim_scores.claim_text: IDF Diabetes Atlas 2024: 73.2% of Indonesian adults with diabetes are unaware of their condition — approximately 15 million undiagnosed cases nationally, third-highest globally
source_categories: primary_association (International Diabetes Federation — Diabetes Atlas 11th ed. 2024)
per_claim_scores.rationale: IDF Diabetes Atlas is the canonical global diabetes epidemiology reference, published by the International Diabetes Federation (a WHO-affiliated umbrella organization). It is primary_association (global health association, not a market research firm). The 2024 edition is the most recent. Two IDF-domain URLs both pointing to the same underlying dataset — counts as one source, but that source is the authoritative primary for global diabetes prevalence data. Indonesia-specific data page cited directly. No geography mismatch. Recent (2024). This is a strong High.

per_claim_scores.claim_text: Retrospective cohort study of Indonesian employer-sponsored retiree health insurance (29,695 retirees, 2020–2023): five diseases with increasing claims trend; cardiovascular disease accounted for 37% of high-cost disease expenditure
per_claim_scores.rationale: Prastyo & Gani 2025 is peer-reviewed (Narra J, PMC12425502), Indonesia-specific, uses actual Indonesian employer-sponsored retiree insurance claims data (2020–2023), large cohort (29,695 retirees). This is the best available academic evidence for the CDM cost burden in Indonesian employer insurance. Strong primary_academic. The limitation — retiree population, not active workforce — should be noted but doesn't invalidate the claim.

per_claim_scores.claim_text: Indonesian TPAs (AdMedika, Owlexa, Meditap, etc.) are compensated per claim and report by benefit category, not by disease cohort; condition-level analytics not bundled in standard TPA contracts
source_categories: secondary_market_research (NextMSC — private market research firm; NEEDS-ATTENDED-FETCH)
per_claim_scores.rationale: Two issues: (1) AdMedika.co.id is the vendor's own website describing its own product/services — auto-Low per vendor-marketing override. (2) NextMSC is a private market research firm (similar to Mordor/MarketsandMarkets category) and flagged NEEDS-ATTENDED-FETCH — unverified. The structural claim about TPA incentive misalignment is plausible and logically coherent, but the sourcing relies on vendor self-description and an unverified market research firm. Auto-Low.

per_claim_scores.claim_text: BPJS JKN and supplemental private employer claims have no interoperability/shared claims file — diabetic employee managing condition via BPJS generates zero employer-TPA claims until a specialist visit
source_categories: primary_academic (PMC6861401 — National Health Insurance Databases Indonesia)
primary_academic (Khoe et al 2024, PMC11308606 — employer insurance provision study)
per_claim_scores.rationale: Two independent peer-reviewed academic sources. PMC6861401 addresses the JKN database structure; Khoe et al 2024 (PMC11308606) covers employer insurance provision. Together they document the architecture of Indonesia's two-tier insurance system and the data gap between tiers. Both Indonesia-specific. Recent (2024 for Khoe; 2019 for PMC6861401 — the 2019 JKN database article is borderline but the structural fact about BPJS/private insurance separation is an enduring regulatory architecture). Two independent primary academic sources. Score: High.

per_claim_scores.claim_text: Incremental cost of adding HbA1c to a standard MCU panel: approximately Rp 75,000–150,000 / USD 5–10 per employee per year based on Prodia Digital and hospital MCU pricing
source_categories: secondary (Prodia Digital — commercial lab's own consumer-facing price list)
secondary (Tirta Medical Centre — MCU provider's own pricing page)
per_claim_scores.rationale: Both sources are MCU/lab provider websites listing their own prices. Prodia is a commercial diagnostic lab; Tirta Medical is a clinic. These are provider-side pricing pages, not independent cost studies. While provider pricing pages are a legitimate way to establish retail pricing (this is not vendor-marketing-override for capability claims — it is pricing data), they are single commercial sources. The claim is plausible but relies on two provider pricing pages. The vendor-marketing override specifically applies to claims about a vendor's capabilities/market; pricing data from a provider's own price list is a borderline case. Scored Low because: (1) no independent cross-check (e.g., BPJS tariff schedule, health economics study); (2) provider pricing can be outdated on websites; (3) single-source-type (both are commercial lab/clinic pricing pages).
overrides_triggered: single-trade-source (operating cost figure from provider price lists only)

per_claim_scores.claim_text: Private hospital inpatient for dialysis initiation: Rp 30M–80M+ per episode (USD 1,935–5,160); BPJS-reported inpatient costs for CKD among Indonesia's top five catastrophic claim categories
source_categories: primary_academic (Value in Health Regional Issues 2016 T2DM cost study — stale)
secondary_unknown (revistas.tec-ac.cr/tec_empresarial — Costa Rican business journal; peer-review status unclear; cited as 'BPJS 2023 T2DM direct cost analysis')
per_claim_scores.rationale: The dialysis episode cost figure (Rp 30M–80M+) is not directly sourced — neither the 2016 Value in Health paper nor the Costa Rican journal article clearly states private hospital dialysis initiation costs. The private hospital episode cost range appears to be the draft author's estimate. The tec_empresarial journal (Costa Rica) as a source for Indonesian BPJS 2023 data is highly suspicious — this journal is not a recognized Indonesian health economics publication. One source is 2016 (stale). The dialysis cost figure lacks a primary citation (no hospital tariff schedule, no BPJS tariff data, no PERSI/hospital association data cited). Auto-Low.
overrides_triggered: unverifiable-source (revistas.tec-ac.cr for Indonesian BPJS data is a significant source quality concern)

per_claim_scores.claim_text: MCU cost per employee for a standard corporate package: Rp 400,000–1,200,000 / USD 26–77 at Tier-1 city providers (Prodia, Kimia Farma, hospital MCU departments)
source_categories: auto_low_vendor (EMC Healthcare — MCU provider describing own pricing)
per_claim_scores.rationale: Three MCU provider pricing pages. EMC Healthcare pricing page is auto-Low (vendor describing own services/pricing). The other two are commercial clinic pricing pages — provider self-reported pricing is secondary at best. No independent cross-check (health ministry schedule, BPJS tariff for comparison). Single-source-type override: all three are commercial MCU provider pricing pages.

per_claim_scores.claim_text: IDF Diabetes Atlas 2024: 73.2% of Indonesian diabetics undiagnosed; among working-age urban adults, undetected share may be slightly lower but remains above 60% based on national survey data
per_claim_scores.rationale: The 73.2% national figure is High-tier (IDF primary association, same as PP1.1-freq-4). However, the 'remains above 60% for urban working-age' qualifier is not directly sourced — it is an inference ('may be slightly lower... but remains above 60% based on national survey data'). The claim bundles a well-sourced figure (73.2%) with an inferential extrapolation (60% for urban working-age). Score: Medium because the quantified extrapolation (60%) is not independently sourced.

per_claim_scores.claim_text: 2024 cost-effectiveness study of community-based T2DM prevention in Indonesia: early detection programs cost-effective at USD 1,200–2,400 per QALY; dominant barrier was access to screening, not treatment efficacy

One source but it is primary and directly relevant. Score: High — the IDF Atlas for prevalence (High) plus this academic cost-effectiveness study make the screening ROI case well-sourced.

The claim about what the regulation does/does not specify is verifiable from the regulation's text. High.

per_claim_scores.claim_text: CHD generates 21.8 missed work days per affected person per year (6.8 absenteeism + 15.0 presenteeism) vs. 10.6 for a general worker; GDP cost of CHD-related productivity loss: US$33.3 billion lifetime for the current 2M CHD-prevalence working-age cohort
source_categories: primary_academic (Uli/Tran et al 2020, BMC Cardiovascular Disorders, PMC7482464 — Indonesia-specific life-table study)
per_claim_scores.rationale: PMC7482464 is peer-reviewed, Indonesia-specific, uses life-table modelling of the working Indonesian population. The specific figures (21.8 missed days, 6.8 absenteeism, 15.0 presenteeism, $33.3B lifetime, 2M CHD prevalence) are all attributable to this paper. Primary academic, recent enough (2020 — borderline on 5-year recency but the modelling data reflects structural long-term burden, not a one-year snapshot). Score: High.

per_claim_scores.claim_text: Singapore total economic cost per working-age diabetic: USD 5,646 in 2010; projected USD 7,791 by 2050, with most increase attributed to productivity losses
source_categories: primary_academic (PMC12777722 — 2025 integrative review of DM workplace impacts)
per_claim_scores.rationale: The Singapore cost figure ($5,646 per diabetic) is used in the draft to support a claim about Indonesian employer cost burden. This is a geography mismatch — Singapore is a high-income city-state with very different healthcare costs, wage levels, and purchasing power from Indonesia. The draft applies this 'conservatively' to Indonesia's wage base, but Singapore per-diabetic costs cannot proxy for Indonesia without adjustment. APAC-as-proxy override: Singapore data being used as a comparator for Indonesia-specific cost estimates. Additionally, the 2010 base year data is 15+ years old. Geography mismatch flag.

per_claim_scores.claim_text: South India outpatient cohort: diabetics averaged 7.48 lost work days/year in absenteeism alone
per_claim_scores.rationale: South India absenteeism data applied to Indonesian workforce context. Geography mismatch: India (lower-middle-income, different labour law, different sick-pay liability, different disease management context) is not a valid proxy for Indonesia without explicit adjustment. The draft explicitly uses this to estimate Indonesian productivity loss ('applied to a 1,000-employee urban workforce'). APAC-as-proxy override triggers. Additionally the paper is from 2018 (PMC5870439 published 2018 — now 7–8 years old for a cost/absenteeism figure).
overrides_triggered: apac-as-proxy (South India data applied to Indonesia)

per_claim_scores.claim_text: Finkelstein et al 2014: aggregate OOP + indirect burden of four NCDs on Indonesian households — Int$4.02 billion in 2010, rising to Int$5.80 billion by 2020; diabetes alone Int$0.81B in 2010, Int$1.27B by 2020
source_categories: primary_academic (Finkelstein et al 2014, Duke-NUS/PLOS ONE, PMC4051736 — Indonesia-specific household NCD burden)
per_claim_scores.rationale: Finkelstein 2014 is peer-reviewed and Indonesia-specific — strong source. However: (1) it covers 2010 actual + 2020 projection, meaning even the 'projected' figures are now 5 years in the past and outdated; (2) the study covers household burden (OOP + indirect) which is a different metric from employer-specific cost burden; (3) outdated-source override applies — a 2014 paper using 2010 data with projections to 2020 is now significantly stale for a market sizing exercise. The figures reflect a snapshot from 14 years ago when Indonesian incomes, healthcare costs, and NCD prevalence were materially lower. Score: Low due to outdated-source override.
overrides_triggered: outdated-source-override (2014 paper; 2010 base data; 2020 projections now past)

per_claim_scores.claim_text: Presenteeism accounts for approximately 78% of total health-related productivity costs; absenteeism ~4%; disability ~18%

Applied to Indonesian context without explicit adjustment. Geography unclear (likely Western markets). Single source for a quantified breakdown (78%/4%/18%) that varies significantly by disease type, country, and measurement methodology. The claim is used to frame Indonesian employer-side cost but the source is not Indonesia-specific. Geography mismatch if the study is non-Indonesia.
overrides_triggered: apac-as-proxy (if source is non-Indonesia, which it appears to be based on PMC7108714 publication context)

cross_stage_note: Per-stage validation only. Final cross-stage citation diversity and consistency check deferred to final validation pass.
gate_reasoning: Stage 1 presents a corpus with meaningful primary-source grounding in its core pain points — the IDF Diabetes Atlas, Prastyo & Gani 2025, the Uli/Tran 2020 CHD productivity study, Permenaker 5/2018, and the Khoe/PMC JKN database papers give Pain Points 1.1, 1.2, and 1.3 a defensible academic spine. The 29% High / 38% Medium / 29% Low distribution signals that roughly a third of claims need upgrading before the corpus can anchor a high-confidence commercial narrative. The three most critical weak clusters are: (1) market sizing — the ≥500 HC employer/worker count is entirely assumed, and the GWP market size relies solely on aggregator market research; (2) operating cost figures — private hospital episode costs for cardiovascular/metabolic complications and dialysis lack primary sourcing (single news source or unverifiable journal); and (3) APAC-as-proxy overuse — Singapore, South India, and Hong Kong/Singapore data are directly applied to Indonesian employer cost modeling without adjustment. Pain Point 1.4's 19% medical trend rate is well-supported (MMB HTS 2025), but the productivity loss section (Pain Point 1.3) relies heavily on non-Indonesia comparators and outdated data. These are not fatal to the research but require targeted deep research on: (a) OJK insurance statistics for GWP; (b) BPJS Kesehatan catastrophic claims data for dialysis/cardiovascular episode costs; and (c) an Indonesia-specific productivity-cost-of-illness source for diabetes, which may require commissioning or finding grey literature from ADB or WHO Indonesia office.
